abstract:
We study the problem of finding a family of diverse minimum edge s-t cuts in a directed weighted graph G. Given integers k and d, the task is to decide whether G contains k minimum s-t cuts C_1, …, C_k such that for any i,j ∈ [k], the number of edges in the symmetric difference C_i △ C_j is at least d.
For d ∈ {1,2}, the problem corresponds to counting minimum s-t cuts in G, which is #P-complete [Provan and Ball, SICOMP 1983]. The problem is also known to be NP-complete already for k = 3 [de Berg, López Martínez, Spieksma, ISAAC 2024]. Our main result shows that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the combined parameter k + d.
The main ingredients of our FPT algorithm build on novel structural properties of diverse minimum s-t cuts and a non-trivial application of the flow-augmentation technique of Kim, Kratsch, Pilipczuk, and Wahlström [JACM 2025].

      Abstract
We study the problem of finding a family of diverse minimum edge s–t cuts in a directed weighted
graph G. Given integers k and d, the task is to decide whether G contains k minimum s–t cuts
C1 , . . . , Ck such that for any i, j ∈ [k], the number of edges in the symmetric difference Ci △ Cj is
at least d.
     For d ∈ {1, 2}, the problem corresponds to counting minimum s–t cuts in G, which is #P-complete
[Provan and Ball, SICOMP 1983]. The problem is also known to be NP-complete already for k = 3
[de Berg, López Martínez, Spieksma, ISAAC 2024]. Our main result shows that the problem is
fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the combined parameter k + d.
     The main ingredients of our FPT algorithm build on novel structural properties of diverse
minimum s–t cuts and a non-trivial application of the flow-augmentation technique of Kim, Kratsch,
Pilipczuk, and Wahlström [JACM 2025].

 1      Introduction
The minimum s–t cut problem is one of the most fundamental and central problems in
graph algorithms. Given a directed graph with designated vertices s and t, the task is to
separate s from t by removing a set of edges of minimum total capacity. This problem is
deeply connected to the theory of network flows, as formalized by the max-flow min-cut
theorem, and to notions of graph connectivity.

        minimum cuts (in P).

            By making use of submodular function minimization, de Berg et al. [7] provided a
        (strongly) polynomial-time algorithm for computing minimum s–t cuts with respect to the
        cov and sum measures of diversity. Interestingly, the computational complexity of the min
        diversity measure appears to be more elusive. As shown by de Berg et al. [7], the problem
        of finding k = 3 minimum s–t cuts under the min diversity measure is already NP-hard.
        Meanwhile, when k = 2, the three measures converge, and the solution is always to take the
        two extremal cuts, i.e., the minimum s–t cut closest to s, and the minimum s–t cut closest to
        t [7]. Our main results shed light on the parameterized complexity of this intriguing measure
        of diversity.


        1.1    Overview of Our Results
        We consider a more general capacitated (weighted) variant of the diverse minimum s–t cuts
        problem defined by de Berg et al. [7]. While the weight of a cut is measured by the total
        capacity of its edges, the diversity between cuts is not measured by capacities, but rather
        by the number of edges in the symmetric difference of their edge sets. Because of that, it
        is convenient to formulate the problem using two cost functions on the edges of the input
        graph. The first cost function c, which we call the capacity, represents the weight of an edge
        and contributes to the total weight of a cut. The second cost function, called the multiplicity,
        arises from the algorithmic process.
            In our algorithm, we contract certain edges of the graph, which may result in a graph
        containing parallel edges. Since we subsequently delete parallel edges, it is necessary to
        preserve their potential contribution both to cut weights and to the diversity measure. To
        maintain the correct contribution of a set of parallel edges to a cut, we update the capacity

1.3    Related work
The structure of minimum cuts has been studied extensively, beginning with the classical
work of Picard and Queyranne, who characterized the full family of minimum cuts in a
network and established their lattice structure [21]. From an algorithmic perspective, Karger
and Stein gave a randomized algorithm for computing global minimum cuts [17]. Wagner
studied a related but distinct notion of diversity by considering the problem of finding k
pairwise-disjoint s–t-cuts of minimum total cost in edge-weighted graphs [26]. More broadly,
diversity has appeared in optimization through the maximum diversity problem, which was
analyzed and modeled via zero–one programming by Kuo et al. [20].
    Recent work has explored diversity across many combinatorial problems, including
minimum cuts [7], matchings [12], vertex cover [4], shortest paths [15], spanning trees [16],
and travelling salesman [8]. Most relevant to our setting, Hanaka et al. recently showed that
finding k pairwise-disjoint global minimum cuts is NP-hard [14], sharply contrasting with
the tractability of classical minimum cut problems and motivating the study of alternative
notions of diversity among minimum cuts.
    Specifically, as mentioned above, de Berg et al. [7] consider all three diversity measures
for Diverse Min s-t-Cuts, proving that the problem is solvable in polynomial-time with
respect to the cov and the sum measure, but NP-hard with respect to the min measure.
They also provide a polynomial-time algorithm for computing disjoint minimum s–t cuts.
    Drabik and Masařík show that diverse solutions for a wide class of vertex problems can
be computed in FPT time parameterized by cliquewidth by extending dynamic programs on
cliquewidth decompositions to support general diversity measures [11].

 5        Conclusion

We conclude by stating some open problems. In our paper, we proved that the Diverse
Min s-t-Cuts problem is FPT when parameterized by k and d. However, the running time
of our algorithm is superexponential. It is natural to ask whether it is possible to do better.
The existing complexity lower bound of de Berg, López Martínez, and Spieksma [7] does not
exclude existence of single-exponential in k and d algorithm. Furthermore, it is interesting to
know whether we can get a substantially better running time for the problem on undirected
graphs, as this case may be easier. In particular, we can contract all residual edges in the
preprocessing step. Then for the obtained instance, it can be shown that either it is a
yes-instance of the problem or the pathwidth of the graph does not exceed kd. Another
natural question is whether Diverse Min s-t-Cuts admits a polynomial kernel for the
parameterization by k and d.
    Further questions concern lower bounds. For d ∈ {1, 2}, Diverse Min s-t-Cuts is
equivalent to deciding whether the input weighted graph has k distinct minimum s–t cuts.
Since the problem of counting minimum s–t cuts is #P-complete by the result of Provan and
Ball [22], we obtain that Diverse Min s-t-Cuts is intractable even if d ∈ {1, 2}. However,
this is not the case when k is polynomial in the graph size because minimum s–t cuts can be
enumerated with polynomial (linear) delay [23, 25]. Is Diverse Min s-t-Cuts NP-complete
in the strong sense for a given constant d ≥ 3, that is, when k is polynomial in n?
    Finally, what can be said for the dual parameterization, that is, when the diversity
measure is the maximum size of the intersection of two cuts? Is the problem FPT in this
case? Notice that the maximum family of disjoint s-t-cuts can be found in polynomial time
by the results of Wagner [26].
